facts: The US-Iran war, which the BBC dates to February, is approaching its five-month mark as of the weekend reporting.
President Trump paused US strikes on Iran for a second consecutive night, with US Ambassador to the UN Mike Waltz saying this was meant to give diplomacy "some space" and "a little bit of room."

The pause follows nearly two weeks of daily US strikes and tit-for-tat attacks that had effectively unraveled a ceasefire reached in June; an Iranian army spokesperson said Tehran had likewise halted its "retaliatory" attacks.
Iran and Oman held technical talks in Tehran on Friday and Saturday over management of the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei.

A CBS News/YouGov poll of 2,193 respondents found nearly 8 in 10 Americans believe the war has been harder for the Trump administration than expected, while about 2 in 10 said it has gone about as smoothly as expected; separately, 57% said they are frustrated by the conflict and 19% said they are optimistic.

Fighting resumed after Iranian forces attacked tankers in the Strait of Hormuz on July 13, prompting the US to resume airstrikes and reinstate a naval blockade on Iranian ports; Iran retaliated with attacks that killed four American soldiers, and subsequent US strikes have killed dozens of people, according to Iran's health ministry.
Oil prices hit $100 a barrel earlier in the week for the first time since May, amid fears over global energy supply tied to the Strait of Hormuz.

Waltz denied that depleted US munitions stockpiles are hurting the war effort, saying the military "has everything that it needs," while blaming former President Biden for the depletion; Trump is scheduled to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the White House on Tuesday, and UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said he would meet US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth this week to discuss the Strait of Hormuz.
ladder.analysis:
The pause in US strikes on Iran marks a tactical shift after nearly two weeks of near-daily attacks that had collapsed a ceasefire agreed in June. That ceasefire had included a US-Iran memorandum of understanding to halt military operations, reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and negotiate an end to the war within 60 days, but it broke down after Iranian attacks on tankers in the strait on July 13 triggered renewed US airstrikes and a naval blockade. The strait, a critical global route for oil and gas shipments, remains the central sticking point, as reflected in this weekend's Iran-Oman technical talks and oil prices reaching $100 a barrel for the first time since May.

The new polling data underscores that the conflict has become a political liability domestically, with large majorities of Americans surprised by its difficulty and expressing frustration rather than optimism. This creates a backdrop of public skepticism against which administration officials are simultaneously defending the war's necessity and disputing reports that stretched munitions stockpiles are constraining military options—an issue with direct bearing on how sustainable an extended campaign, or a resumed one after the pause, would be.

dem: Critics have pointed to New York Times reporting, cited by the BBC, that administration officials privately warned expanding hostilities could dangerously drain a diminished stockpile of air defense munitions—raising questions about the war's sustainability that Ambassador Waltz was pressed to rebut.

Given that CBS/YouGov polling shows 57% of Americans frustrated and only 19% optimistic about the war, with nearly 8 in 10 saying it has gone worse than the administration expected, critics argue the conflict lacks public buy-in and question whether the administration has a clear plan for ending it.
rep: Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) argued the US should not "cut and run" from Iran, instead urging continued blockade and strikes, saying Trump likes the daily strikes and that "sometimes you have to kill a few chickens to scare the monkeys."

Rep. Byron Donalds (R-Fla.) defended Trump's handling of the war despite its unpopularity, arguing that while no American wants another military conflict, Trump would be "derelict in his duty" if Iran obtained a nuclear weapon.

Ambassador Mike Waltz maintained the US military "has everything that it needs" to conduct the campaign effectively, attributing any stockpile depletion to the Biden administration rather than current strategy.

ladder.steelman: Both the war's unpopularity at home and the debate over munitions stockpiles point to the same underlying question—whether the current pause reflects a genuine step toward de-escalation and negotiated resolution over the Strait of Hormuz, or merely a tactical breather before further strikes resume, with the answer shaping both the war's human and economic costs and its political durability.
ladder.implications: The coming days—featuring Trump's Tuesday meeting with Netanyahu, continued Iran-Oman talks on the Strait of Hormuz, and UK-US defense consultations—will likely signal whether the pause becomes a durable step toward de-escalation or a brief interlude before strikes resume, with oil markets and munitions availability remaining key pressure points either way.

facts: The 2026 midterm elections are 100 days away as of this reporting, with House Republicans holding a 218-212 majority (one independent, four vacancies) and Senate Republicans holding a 53-47 majority (including two independents who caucus with Democrats).
Every House seat and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot in November 2026; Democrats need a net gain of six House seats and four Senate seats to reclaim majority control of each chamber.

A Fox News poll released this week showed 53% of voters would back the Democratic House candidate versus 46% for the Republican, a gap just outside the margin of error and the highest share either party has recorded in Fox News polling since 1996; Democrats led by 5 points in an April survey.
FEC filings show the RNC with roughly $125.5 million cash on hand compared to about $14.9 million for the DNC, which is also carrying approximately $18 million in debt.
Mid-decade redistricting changes, including in Florida and Texas, gave Republicans a net gain of roughly 10 additional right-leaning congressional districts.
Republicans currently hold 26 governorships to Democrats' 24, with 36 states electing governors in November 2026.

Before recess, House Republicans passed a $95 billion budget blueprint including war-related spending along party lines, along with an increased military budget and new voting-restriction measures; four Republicans joined Democrats to pass a symbolic war-powers resolution calling for troop withdrawal from combat with Iran.
Senate battlegrounds cited by both parties include Alaska, North Carolina, Ohio and Maine, where Republicans are defending seats.
ladder.analysis: The story marks the formal start of the 100-day sprint to the 2026 midterms, a period in which control of the House, Senate and a majority of governorships will be decided. Historically, the party that holds the White House tends to lose seats in midterm elections, a dynamic both parties acknowledge shapes this cycle. Republicans are relying on redistricting gains, a financial edge for their national party committee, and efforts to link Democrats to socialist-aligned primary winners, while Democrats are emphasizing affordability messaging and pointing to polling showing voter dissatisfaction with the economy and the party in power. The outcome will also determine whether President Trump governs with a Republican trifecta or faces divided government, and gubernatorial results will influence redistricting and election administration for years to come.

dem: DCCC spokesperson Nebeyatt Betre argued House Republicans have 'bled Americans' wallets dry with their cost-raising agenda' and said Democrats aim to hold vulnerable House Republicans accountable on affordability.

Rep. Jason Crow said constituents will confront Republican lawmakers over lost healthcare, homes, farms and small businesses, framing the affordability agenda as central to Democrats' path back to power.
DGA Chair Andy Beshear said Trump and Republican gubernatorial candidates have pursued a 'harmful, cost-raising agenda' that restricts freedoms, contrasting it with Democratic governors' record.
rep: RNC Chair Joe Gruters credited Trump-era policies—tax cuts, no tax on tips or overtime, and border enforcement—with reversing what he described as high inflation and gas prices under the Biden administration.

NRSC's Bernadette Breslin and NRCC's Mike Marinella argued Democrats are shifting toward socialism, citing DSA-aligned primary wins, and said the party will spend the next 100 days answering for that record rather than backing border security, voter ID or tax relief.

RGA spokesperson Kollin Crompton said Republican governors are 'leading the nation in jobs, wage growth, affordability, safety, and opportunity' compared with Democratic-led states, framing the contrast as 'common sense versus crazy.'

ladder.steelman: Both parties are reading the same volatile data—poor approval ratings, historic midterm headwinds, a financial mismatch between national committees, and internal party divisions (a socialist-aligned insurgency unsettling Democratic leadership, and a redistricting/spending rift among Republicans)—yet drawing opposite tactical conclusions about who benefits, underscoring how contested the underlying narrative of the election remains.
ladder.implications: Over the next 100 days, both parties will pour resources into a small number of Senate races (Alaska, North Carolina, Ohio, Maine) and dozens of House and gubernatorial contests that will determine not only congressional control but also the shape of future redistricting and state election administration. Internal party tensions—Democratic establishment friction with socialist-aligned primary winners, and Republican disagreements over legislative strategy and war-powers votes—could influence which candidates emerge and how each party's message is received by voters focused on affordability and economic conditions.

facts: The Maine Democratic Party nominated Troy Jackson at a rare nominating convention to replace Graham Platner as its U.S. Senate candidate against Republican incumbent Susan Collins.
Platner withdrew from the race earlier this month after a series of scandals.
Jackson is a former president of the Maine State Senate, a fifth-generation logger from Allagash, and a union organizer who has held legislative office in Maine for more than two decades.
Jackson finished third among five candidates in the Democratic gubernatorial primary held in June before being selected for the Senate race.
Jackson's political career began after he and other loggers blockaded a U.S.-Canada border crossing in 1998 to protest the use of Canadian woodcutters in Maine timberlands.
Collins chairs the Senate Appropriations Committee and is the only Republican Senate incumbent up for reelection in 2026 in a state that Kamala Harris won in 2024.
Democrats need to win the Maine Senate seat to have a chance at a Senate majority in 2026.

Collins' campaign issued a statement calling Jackson 'handpicked by party insiders' and criticizing his Medicare for All position; the Republican National Committee separately called him a 'Bernie Bro' who wants to 'shove socialism down the throats of Maine voters.'
ladder.analysis: Jackson's nomination fills a vacancy created by Platner's scandal-driven exit and hands Maine Democrats a candidate whose working-class biography — a poor, rural upbringing and decades as a logger and union organizer — is harder for opponents to attack than Platner's, given reporting that questioned Platner's own working-class narrative due to his prep-school background and family means. The race matters beyond Maine because Collins is the only Republican Senate incumbent defending a seat in a state won by the Democratic presidential nominee in 2024, making the contest central to whether Democrats can retake the Senate majority. Collins brings institutional advantages — including her Appropriations Committee chairmanship, which channels federal money to a small, low-income state — along with a strong fundraising history and a track record of winning competitive races, while Jackson enters as a newly minted nominee with an untested statewide fundraising operation.

dem: Democrats argue Jackson's authentic working-class background — a childhood shaped by poverty and manual labor — lets him credibly make an affordability argument against Collins amid inflation, tariffs, and rising gas and food prices.

Party supporters contend Jackson can tie Collins to the Trump administration and unpopular policies, including Medicaid cuts, rural hospital closures, and the conservative Supreme Court majority that overturned Roe v. Wade.

Democrats point to Jackson's platform, including Medicare for All, as evidence the party's energy lies in working-class populism, following the momentum Platner had built around similar Bernie Sanders-aligned positions.
rep: Collins' campaign argues Jackson was 'handpicked by party insiders' rather than chosen through a broader competitive process, and warns his Medicare for All proposal would burden low- and middle-income Mainers with higher costs.
The Republican National Committee frames Jackson as a 'Bernie Bro' seeking to impose socialism on Maine voters, aiming to define him ideologically before he can introduce himself statewide.

Republicans are expected to leverage Collins' structural advantages — her Appropriations Committee chairmanship, prior record of winning tough races, and greater financial resources — as reasons she can withstand a well-funded Democratic challenge.

ladder.steelman: Both parties are contesting the same terrain — who can credibly claim the 'working-class' mantle in a small, economically strained state — with Democrats betting Jackson's harder-to-discredit biography neutralizes the attacks that damaged Platner, while Republicans bet that ideological labeling and Collins' institutional advantages will outweigh any authenticity edge.
ladder.implications: With roughly 100 days until the midterms, the race will test whether a genuinely working-class Democratic nominee with less name recognition and fundraising capacity than his predecessor can overcome an entrenched incumbent's institutional advantages in a state Democrats view as essential to a Senate majority, while Republicans work quickly to define Jackson ideologically before he can build a statewide profile.

facts: A cyclosporiasis outbreak, which has sickened thousands and can cause severe gastrointestinal illness, has been linked to iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms de Mexico.

Former FDA Commissioner Dr. Scott Gottlieb said Sunday on CBS's Face the Nation that the outbreak is not yet under control, though he said the FDA has done a good job isolating it to central Mexico and specific farms.

According to a Wall Street Journal report cited by Gottlieb and The Guardian, Taylor Farms contacted the White House to request more time before federal investigators publicly linked the company to the outbreak, and the White House asked FDA officials to join that call.

During the call, Taylor Farms argued that investigators lacked positive laboratory evidence tying its products to the outbreak and expressed concern that the government was overstating the company's responsibility, per the Journal's reporting.
Gottlieb said such direct outreach to the White House was 'not standard operating procedure,' including during his own tenure handling E. coli outbreaks in spinach and romaine lettuce.

The FDA issued an update saying lettuce not covered by the recall had tested positive for cyclospora, then deleted that statement a day later, calling the test result a false positive while maintaining the recall remained in effect.

Taylor Farms posted a statement saying the FDA had apologized to the company and that FDA had not identified a single positive product test result for cyclospora, though there was no public confirmation of an FDA apology.
Taylor Farms later clarified that its recall remained in effect and that it would no longer source iceberg lettuce from central Mexico for the current growing season.
ladder.analysis: Cyclosporiasis is a foodborne illness caused by a parasite that has, in this case, been traced to iceberg lettuce grown in central Mexico and supplied by Taylor Farms de Mexico. The episode has drawn scrutiny not just for the scale of illness but for how federal officials and the company communicated about it: the FDA published, then retracted, a finding of contamination in non-recalled product, and Taylor Farms made public claims about an FDA apology that were not independently confirmed. Layered on top of these communication stumbles is a reported effort by Taylor Farms to enlist White House involvement before the recall was publicly announced — an approach a former FDA commissioner says departs from typical practice, where companies work directly with the agency rather than routing concerns through the White House.

dem: Some Democrats and food-safety advocates could point to the Taylor Farms–White House contact as evidence of undue corporate access to political leadership during a public-health decision, echoing broader concerns about regulatory capture.

Democrats might argue the FDA's flip-flopping public statements — publishing then retracting a positive test result — reflect a breakdown in transparency that puts consumer trust and safety at risk, warranting stronger oversight of how recalls are communicated.
rep: Some Republicans could argue that a company seeking clarity from regulators before a potentially costly recall is a legitimate business concern, especially if, as Taylor Farms claimed, no positive product test result had been identified at the time.

Republicans skeptical of regulatory overreach might frame the FDA's retracted false-positive announcement as evidence of agency dysfunction that unfairly damaged a company's reputation before the science was settled, rather than focusing criticism on the company's outreach to the White House.

ladder.steelman: Regardless of political framing, the episode is fundamentally a story about a breakdown in clear, consistent communication between a federal regulator and the public during an active health crisis — a failure that undermines confidence in the recall process whether the underlying concern is corporate influence or regulatory overreach.
ladder.implications: The unresolved status of the outbreak and unanswered questions about the Taylor Farms–White House contact are likely to prompt further reporting, potential congressional inquiries into FDA communication protocols, and continued scrutiny of how recall announcements are coordinated between regulators, companies, and the executive branch.

facts: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) faces a packed legislative agenda this week, with government funding as his top priority.
Senate appropriators remain deadlocked over top-line spending levels for government funding legislation.
Thune is considering a stopgap measure (continuing resolution) to keep federal agencies funded past the current deadline.
The government funding deadline is the end of September, after which a shutdown could occur without a deal.
Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) said publicly on Sunday that Thune is 'being too cautious' in his talks with Senate Democratic leaders aimed at avoiding a shutdown.
Thune is also under pressure from President Trump to advance a third reconciliation bill.
The Senate is in its final two weeks before an extended recess, compressing the timeline for both funding and reconciliation work.
ladder.analysis: Thune's position illustrates the structural squeeze facing Senate GOP leadership: government funding bills require 60 votes to clear procedural hurdles, forcing negotiation with Senate Democrats even though Republicans hold the majority, while reconciliation bills can pass with a simple majority but require intra-party consensus that has proven elusive on spending levels. The approaching recess adds a hard deadline to both tracks, meaning delays on one issue could crowd out time needed for the other. This dual pressure — bipartisan dealmaking on funding paired with unified-party pressure on reconciliation — is a recurring dynamic in periods of narrow majorities and looming shutdown deadlines.

dem: Because government funding legislation needs Democratic votes to overcome the Senate's 60-vote threshold, Senate Democratic leaders are positioned to extract concessions on spending levels during negotiations with Thune, a dynamic reflected in the ongoing appropriations deadlock.
rep: Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) argues Thune's cautious, negotiation-heavy approach with Democrats risks losing leverage and that a firmer posture would better serve Republican priorities heading into the shutdown deadline.
President Trump is pushing Thune to prioritize and expedite a third reconciliation bill, reflecting a wing of the party that wants aggressive action on GOP priorities even as funding talks continue.

ladder.steelman: Thune is caught between two competing imperatives — needing Democratic cooperation to avoid a shutdown while facing Republican and Trump pressure to move unilaterally on reconciliation — and satisfying one track risks undermining momentum on the other, all within a shrinking legislative calendar before recess.
ladder.implications: With roughly two weeks left before the Senate's extended recess and a shutdown deadline at the end of September, Thune's handling of the stopgap funding measure and the pace of reconciliation talks will likely determine whether Republicans avoid a funding lapse and whether intra-party friction — exemplified by Kennedy's public criticism — hardens into a broader leadership challenge.

stories.headline: Berlin Pride ramming suspect shot dead by police after manhunt
body: German police shot and killed Abdul Ballout, the 21-year-old suspect in a deadly vehicle-ramming and stabbing attack at Berlin's Christopher Street Day Pride event, ending a 24-hour manhunt on Sunday evening. Ballout, a German citizen of Lebanese heritage, was located at an allotment garden complex in the Spandau district and rushed at officers with a bladed weapon, prompting police to open fire, authorities said. He died at the scene despite resuscitation efforts.

The attack occurred around 10:00 p.m. local time Saturday in Tiergarten park near the Brandenburg Gate, where hundreds of thousands had gathered for the annual Pride celebration. A white van drove into a crowd, killing one woman and injuring at least 29 people, several severely. After the vehicle crashed into a tree, the driver fled on foot, and officials said he then attacked additional people with a blade, possibly a machete. By Sunday afternoon, police confirmed none of the injured remained in life-threatening condition.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said evidence indicated the attack was likely an "Islamist terror attack." Ballout was known to authorities for a "high number" of prior criminal offenses, radicalization, and affiliation with Islamist circles. According to the Berlin public prosecutor's office, Ballout traveled to Lebanon in May 2025 intending to join the Islamic State group in Syria, was arrested there, and sentenced to three months for incitement. After returning to Germany in November 2025, he was detained and in May 2026 received a suspended sentence of one year and 10 months for "preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state," with supervision by a parole officer. He had prior convictions for assault and robbery.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the attack scene and later spoke at a church service, pledging to "defend the freedom and openness of our lives" and stating that "these extremists have no place in our society." Berlin Mayor Kai Wegner called the attack "an attack on our free and cosmopolitan society" and praised police for locating the suspect within 24 hours. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen expressed sympathy, saying the Pride event stands for "freedom, dignity, and equality."

Dobrindt said Germany's threat level would be raised following the attack, and other states were advised to review security measures for major events. The Federal Public Prosecutor General will take over the investigation. Hundreds of mourners gathered at the Brandenburg Gate for an impromptu vigil, where speakers condemned extremism but also criticized recent budget cuts for queer organizations. Saturday's attack is the latest in a string of deadly vehicle-ramming incidents in Germany and worldwide in recent years, including attacks in Leipzig, Mannheim, Munich, and the 2016 Berlin Christmas market attack.

stories.headline: US and Iran pause strikes for second day amid diplomatic push
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: The United States and Iran have paused military strikes for a second consecutive day, marking the first sustained break in hostilities after nearly two weeks of nightly attacks. The relative calm comes as diplomatic efforts intensify to revive an interim ceasefire deal signed in mid-June, which has been largely undermined by the recent exchanges of fire. US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz told Fox News on Sunday that President Donald Trump was 'giving [the potential for] talks … a little bit of room,' while noting that negotiators have been engaged at every level over the past few days.

US broadcaster CBS, citing two regional sources, reported that the decision to pause the bombing was linked to the arrival of an Omani delegation in Tehran. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei told Austrian broadcaster ORF that mediators including Qatar and Pakistan are exchanging messages between the two countries, and that talks with Oman about managing traffic in the Strait of Hormuz were 'useful, and progress was made.' However, Baghaei added that Iran’s past efforts at diplomacy have been 'betrayed,' reflecting lingering mistrust. A senior Iranian official, speaking anonymously to Reuters, said Iran’s position remains 'attack for attack' and that the pause is viewed as 'tactical rather than genuine.'

The New York Times reported that Trump paused plans to escalate attacks due to concerns about draining the Pentagon’s diminishing stockpile of missile interceptors and other air defense munitions in the Middle East. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Trump 'has always been consistent in saying he prefers a diplomatic solution, but he continues to retain all options if Iran continues terrorist activities in the Strait of Hormuz or against allies.' Iran’s army spokesman Mohammad Akraminia said Iran had halted its retaliatory operations, but warned that the conflict would widen further if the US continues its attacks.

The pause follows two weeks of escalating conflict that began with Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a key global energy route. The US responded with nightly strikes on Iranian coastal areas and infrastructure, while Iran counterattacked against countries hosting US military forces, killing at least three at a base in Jordan. The US military’s Central Command said its naval blockade of Iran 'remains in full effect,' reporting that as of Saturday it had redirected 12 commercial vessels, disabled two, and boarded two. Iranian media reported that the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps stopped six vessels by firing warning shots, and that an oil tanker exploded after hitting a mine in the strait.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, set to meet with Trump in Washington on Tuesday, told Fox News he 'fully' backs Trump’s efforts to weaken Iran and press it to end its nuclear program, adding that if Iran again attacks Israel, 'it will make a terrible mistake.' A regional official involved in mediation said the pause is a 'positive signal' and that a compromise being negotiated centers on having Iran manage vessel transit through the Strait of Hormuz with fewer restrictions. A poll by Ipsos and The Washington Post found that only 29 percent of Americans surveyed approve of Trump’s handling of the war with Iran, and 28 percent say the war was worth it, underscoring growing domestic pressure on the president to find an exit strategy.

stories.headline: Israeli settlers set fire to mosques and farmland in West Bank
body: Israeli settlers set fire to two mosques, cars and agricultural land in the occupied West Bank overnight, Palestinian officials said, as tensions in the territory continue to escalate. The attacks targeted the villages of Qusra and Kour, with settlers spray-painting graffiti that included the word 'revenge' on the walls of one mosque, according to the mayor of Qusra, Abdul Azim Wadi. The Israeli military said troops were sent to Qusra and that police would investigate and collect evidence.

The latest incidents come two days after a clash between settlers and Palestinians near the village of Tal, which left four Palestinians and two Israelis dead. Both sides accused the other of provoking the violence. Since that deadly confrontation, Palestinians say there have been multiple settler attacks on villages across the West Bank. In the village of Sarra, residents said six buildings were torched and more than a dozen others attacked with stones. Hanan Turabi, a resident, described seeing crowds of settlers running toward her house and fleeing with her four children at the last second. 'They came from everywhere,' she said. 'We tried to escape but they followed us and threw stones.' Kaied Ahmad Turabi, visiting from Miami, was treated for injuries including a head wound that required 12 stitches. 'They came ready,' he said of the attackers, who he said had covered faces and carried sticks.

The violence has drawn international condemnation but shown little sign of being reversed. The United Nations says 1,114 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023, the vast majority by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), and at least 35 of those deaths have involved attacks by settlers. It says 41 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations in the West Bank in the same period. The IDF has carried out raids and arrested more than 130 individuals over the weekend in what it called a 'counter-terrorism' operation.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu responded to the Tal incident by vowing to take 'powerful action,' including the possible demolition of the homes of two Palestinians allegedly involved. He also said he would speed up the establishment and legalisation of farm outposts in the West Bank. New Israeli outposts have already appeared in the area since then, including one near Sarra visible from the main road. Israel's military said it was working to prevent 'incidents of nationalist crime'—its term for attacks by extremist settlers. The settlements, which house about 700,000 Jews alongside an estimated 3.3 million Palestinians, are illegal under international law. Palestinian officials say at least 45 mosques have been vandalised or burned by settlers since 2025.

stories.headline: Tens of thousands evacuated as wildfires rage across Europe and North Africa
body: Tens of thousands of people have been evacuated from their homes as wildfires continue to rage across parts of Europe and North Africa, with France and Spain among the hardest-hit countries. In France, approximately 55,000 people were evacuated overnight into Sunday from villages south of Bordeaux in the Gironde region, bringing the total number of evacuees in the country's southwest to more than 220,000, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez. In Spain, more than 90,000 people have been evacuated from regions around Madrid and Ávila, with additional evacuations near Valencia. Across both countries, more than 330,000 people have been forced to flee.

The fires in France's Gironde region, famed for its vineyards, have burned about 42,000 hectares, making it one of the largest forest fires since World War Two, officials said. Nationwide, approximately 98,000 hectares have burned since the start of the year, a historic record, Nuñez said Saturday. In Spain, around 77,000 hectares have been affected, according to Minister for Ecological Transition Sara Aagesen, who described the wildfire in the Ávila region as the largest in the country's recent history. More than 150 houses have been destroyed in the French coastal town of Le Porge alone.

Firefighting efforts in France involve 2,500 firefighters, including a Swiss team, 1,500 military personnel, and nearly 1,200 police and gendarmes. Captain Nicolas Braz, a leader of the firefighting operation, said the fire had created "its own winds - complete with whirlwinds," adding it was "erratic and unmanageable." In Spain, Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska declared a national state of emergency. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said "difficult hours lie ahead" but noted "positive" indications overnight toward containing the blaze near Madrid, and called for "a major public pact on the climate emergency."

The fires have also disrupted transportation and events. Bordeaux Airport reported delays to every flight from Sunday afternoon onward, with air traffic control restrictions put in place to facilitate emergency services. The final stage of the Tour de France was shortened from 133 km to 89 km to allow security forces to be redeployed to the firefighting effort. In North Africa, extreme heat and strong winds are fueling wildfires in Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco, with Tunisia calling in international firefighting aircraft to battle fires threatening forests, farmland, and communities.

At least one civilian has been killed in a smaller fire in Spain's Valencia region, and two firefighters were killed earlier in the week fighting the blaze near Bordeaux. Residents in affected areas have organized volunteer networks to support firefighters. "I think many of them have never experienced a fire of this magnitude before," said Nathalie Augonnet, a volunteer in Le Porge. French President Emmanuel Macron said France would "rebuild" and his government would "be there for as long as is needed." The World Health Organization has warned that climate change is contributing to the frequency and intensity of such fires, as record temperatures and successive heatwaves have been seen across Europe since May.

stories.headline: Israel approves international stabilisation force for Gaza
body: Israel’s government has approved the entry of the International Stabilization Force (ISF) into Gaza, part of US President Donald Trump’s 20-point “peace plan,” an Israeli official reported on Sunday. The security cabinet approved key legal measures for the force, which will operate “in full coordination with” the Israeli military, according to the Times of Israel. No timeframe was given for deployment.

The ISF will include 200 personnel from “friendly countries such as Uganda and Morocco,” according to Reuters. The cabinet determined that Israel will have the authority to approve which countries can send forces. The force will operate in areas of the Palestinian enclave that are outside Israel’s military control. Israel currently occupies close to 70 percent of Gaza, and its population of almost two million has been forced to live in a diminishing fraction of the strip as Israel continues to move the “Yellow Line” demarcating areas it withdrew to under the first phase of the ceasefire deal.

The plan also calls for an international “Board of Peace” to oversee the administration and reconstruction of the strip, the creation of a National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG) technocratic governing body, and for Hamas to disarm and Israel to withdraw from the strip. Nickolay Mladenov, director-general of the Gaza Board of Peace – which the vast majority of Western countries refused to join – welcomed the news. He said Israel enabling the deployment was “a critical part of the agreed framework for stabilising Gaza, supporting demilitarisation, and enabling the transition to effective Palestinian transitional administration” under the NCAG.

Though a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel was agreed in October, reports of killings of Palestinians by the Israeli military occur almost daily. The Palestinian Ministry of Health reports that 1,200 Palestinians have been killed since the deal was implemented, with 3,888 wounded. Following implementation of Trump’s deal, Israel dictates who can and cannot enter the Gaza Strip, along with how much aid and food can enter, in the wake of Israel’s two-year, genocidal war on Gaza.

Displaced Palestinians in Gaza cautiously welcomed the approval, hoping the force can help rebuild Gaza and allow them to return home after months of bombardment and displacement. The cabinet’s approval comes a day before Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is due to travel to Washington, DC.

stories.headline: U.S. and Iran Pause Attacks, Oil Prices Drop and Stock Futures Rally
body: U.S. stock-index futures rallied and oil prices tumbled on Sunday as the U.S. and Iran took a pause from fighting, with Wall Street also preparing for the Federal Reserve’s meeting this week and a wave of Big Tech earnings reports, led by Apple.

The pause marks a reversal after a period of heightened tensions that saw the collapse of a three-week U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding, a return of hostilities, and Brent crude oil prices soaring past $100 per barrel. The escalation included Houthi strikes on two Saudi tankers in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a chokepoint that had been handling 4 to 5 million barrels per day of Saudi oil and which Saudi Arabia was using as its primary export route due to the Iranian blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Tankers heading to the Red Sea made U-turns for longer, costlier routes, and the strait now appears almost completely blocked. The Strait of Hormuz, which once saw average daily volumes of 20 million barrels, slowed to a trickle. Simultaneously, Ukrainian drone strikes on the Caspian Pipeline System’s Black Sea terminus at Novorossiysk forced Kazakhstan to suspend most of its oil exports, removing an additional 1.7 million barrels per day from global markets. Tanker operators grew nervous about sending vessels to Novorossiysk as drones also struck ships at the port, according to Bloomberg. Ukrainian forces continued to target Russian refineries, leading to a temporary ban on diesel exports. The multiple supply disruptions prompted warnings of a possible global recession.

The disruptions had severe consequences for U.S. airlines, which faced soaring jet fuel costs. The U.S. jet fuel market had been tightening since March, and the renewed hostilities pushed Brent crude back above $100, further bloating fuel expenses. U.S. exports of jet fuel, gasoline, and diesel hit record highs as refining margins soared amid constrained crude supply at the Strait of Hormuz. Global fuel markets tightened, and prices spiked during peak summer travel demand, though Europe avoided the shortages that had been feared. Jet fuel stocks on the West Coast, which relies more on imports than other U.S. regions, were under particular stress. In response, Southwest Airlines chartered a vessel to ship 12.6 million gallons of jet fuel from Houston to Los Angeles via the Panama Canal, made possible by a Trump Administration waiver of the Jones Act. "It brought like a week's supply to the West Coast at a time when supply was most constricted ... when it was most at risk," Southwest chief financial officer Tom Doxey told CNBC. The shipment arrived at the end of May. Despite reporting consensus-beating second-quarter earnings, Southwest noted its fuel expenses jumped $900 million year-over-year. The fuel price rally in the past two weeks prompted all U.S. carriers to adjust their 2026 earnings expectations lower.

The oil market’s earlier narrative of a looming glut has been upended by the multiple supply disruptions. "Unlike crude oil, refined products face far fewer mitigation options," said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank. "Several Middle Eastern refineries remain affected by the ongoing conflict while Russia’s diesel export restrictions continue to constrain global availability. Refining capacity globally also remains relatively limited, preventing crude supply increases from quickly translating into additional diesel and gasoline production."

The pause in attacks provided immediate relief to markets, with oil prices diving and stock futures rising. However, underlying tensions remain, and the situation at key chokepoints continues to constrain supply. Investors now turn their attention to the Fed’s monetary policy meeting and a wave of Big Tech earnings, with Apple leading the reports.

stories.headline: Fed Faces Growing Pressure to Hike Rates as Treasury Yields Rise
body: The Federal Reserve, under Chair Kevin Warsh, is facing mounting pressure to raise interest rates as Treasury yields rise, signaling that markets are "enormously worried" about inflation, according to MarketWatch. The rising yields reflect a clear warning from the Treasury market that the Fed must back up its tough talk on inflation with concrete action.

Bloomberg reports that the Fed faces growing pressure to hike rates as price risks rebound. The new Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, has not publicly disclosed his views on the matter, with The Washington Post noting that he "won’t tell you what he thinks." This opacity comes at a time when market participants are closely watching for signals on the central bank's next move.

Modern Ghana adds that the Federal Reserve is due to make another decision on interest rates, though no specific date or details are provided in the source material. The combination of rising Treasury yields and rebounding price risks has intensified the debate over whether the Fed will act to curb inflationary pressures.

The stakes are high: if the Fed fails to follow through on its hawkish rhetoric, markets may interpret that as a lack of commitment to price stability, potentially fueling further inflation expectations. Conversely, a rate hike could calm bond markets but risk slowing economic growth. The next Fed decision will be closely watched for any shift in tone or policy direction.

stories.headline: Pogacar wins fifth Tour de France title amid Paris finish drama
body: Slovenian Tadej Pogacar won the Tour de France for a record-equalling fifth time on Sunday, crossing the line on Paris' Champs-Élysées in the peloton to join Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain as the endurance event's most successful male riders. The 27-year-old UAE Team Emirates-XRG rider described his achievement as "something you wouldn't even maybe write in a story book."

The final stage was won by the Netherlands' Mathieu van der Poel of Alpecin-Premier Tech after a frantic charge to the line on the famous cobbles, in which he pipped team-mate Jasper Philipsen of Belgium by inches. Van der Poel, a classics legend with multiple victories in Paris-Roubaix and the Tour of Flanders, added this prestigious victory to his collection, saying: "We have a saying in Dutch that it has to come for your toes. I don't know where this came from, but not from my toes." The stage was reduced from 133km to 89km after the redirection of emergency services to help tackle wildfires in south-west France.

Pogacar's victory marks his third Tour win in succession and includes a record-breaking ascent of the iconic Alpe d'Huez on stage 19, when he sealed another dominant victory. It was the last of five stage wins in a race in which Pogacar used his explosive launch and unmatchable metronomic pace to see off his rivals. He now has 127 wins in an eight-year elite professional career and has won almost every major race in the sport, including the Tour of Flanders, Giro d'Italia, Milan-San Remo, Road World Championships, Giro di Lombardia and Liège-Bastogne-Liège.

Pogacar's only real rival in this year's race was the much-improved Belgian Remco Evenepoel of Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe, who finished six minutes 26 seconds behind overall. Third place went to Pogacar's Mexican team-mate Isaac del Toro, who won stage two thanks largely to Pogacar's babysitting pace. The one rider who has broken Pogacar's stranglehold of cycling's biggest race in the past was Denmark's Jonas Vingegaard, who won in 2022 and 2023, but this year the 29-year-old Visma-Lease a Bike rider abandoned after breaking his collarbone on a right-hand bend on stage 15. The mistake was very unlike Vingegaard's near-perfect technique, and attention soon turned to scrutiny of the International Testing Agency, which had awoken Vingegaard at 2am to carry out an anti-doping test. Other riders had the same treatment, including Pogacar at 5am, but the ITA said there were "exceptional circumstances" to take the night tests, which are rare and require additional permission. It is not known when the test results will be published.

Pogacar was booed by some fans during the Tour, as his performances are often so far ahead of any of his peers that some feel frustrated the sport is losing its competitive edge. "Victory is really special," said Pogacar. "Thank you to all the fans and my team. But the biggest thanks goes to all my family who support me all my life. My parents - without them I would not be standing here five times already. Seven Tours and seven times on the podium, and five wins, is something you wouldn't even maybe write in a story book, and it's unbelievable for me. It's a magnificent podium with some incredible champions to fight with. It's a shame Jonas [Vingegaard] crashed out this time and many others. I hope they have a quick recovery and next year we fight again."

In the year when Britain's four-time Tour winner Chris Froome retired, his former team - now known as Netcompany Ineos Cycling - failed to record a stage victory in 21 attempts. Ex-Ineos rider Tom Pidcock of Pinarello-Q36.5 did not manage to win a stage, but he and his team will be satisfied with his consistent battling riding, which earned him ninth in the general classification. Fellow Briton Adam Yates, 33, showed great tenacity after falling ill on stage 16 and spending two days riding at the back of the field before helping pace Pogacar up a climb for victory on stage 19. The green points jersey was awarded to Denmark's Mads Pedersen of Lidl-Trek, and the king of the mountains' polka dot jersey went to Ecuador's Richard Carapaz of EF Education-Easypost.

stories.headline: Littler and Greaves win World Matchplay titles
body: Luke Littler defended his World Matchplay title in sensational style, smashing Phil Taylor's tournament and final average records in the process. The 19-year-old world number one beat seventh seed Gerwyn Price 18-9 in Blackpool to become just the fourth person to win back-to-back Matchplay titles. Littler finished the week with an average of 111.04, beating Taylor's record of 106.31 from 2010, and averaged 111.53 in the final, bettering Taylor's 111.23 against Adrian Lewis in 2013. He claimed £225,000 in prize money and now leads the PDC's two-year order of merit with £3,143,500, £2.13m ahead of second-placed Luke Humphries.

Littler went into the final as the overwhelming favourite and a stunning 167 finish in the fourth leg secured an early break to help him take the first mini-session 4-1. He led 8-2 with an average of 114.74, approaching Taylor's record of 114.99 in any Matchplay game. His level dropped slightly in the next two sessions but he still won both 3-2, moving within two legs with a 148 checkout — his sixth ton-plus finish in the final — before a break and hold sealed his fourth ranking title of the calendar year. Littler also hit 12 180s in the final, setting a new tournament record of 66, surpassing the total he set last year. The win extended his streak of successive victories in matches of 20 or more legs to 29; his last defeat in such a match was the 2024 World Championship final against Luke Humphries.

"It's been a crazy week, one of the best weeks of my life with the darts I've played," Littler told Sky Sports. "It's been tough, the stats may look like it's easy but when you're on this stage with how hit it is, it's not easy." Price, who averaged 104.97 in the final, climbed to fourth in the order of merit and reclaimed the Welsh number one spot from Jonny Clayton. "Luke is one in a million, I threw everything at him," Price said. "He's fantastic for the sport. I wish he wasn't as good as he is — I would have won a couple more tournaments. I hope there's no-one else like him coming through because he's ridiculous!"

Littler reiterated his intention to attempt a clean sweep of PDC ranking titles in the calendar year, a feat never achieved. The Players Championship Finals in November are a sticking point, requiring him to play in — and likely win — some Pro Tour events to qualify. He has skipped the first 24 Pro Tour events and pulled out of the two in Hildesheim this week, leaving eight left. A win is worth £15,000 and a runner-up spot £10,000; the final qualifying spot currently has £22,750 in prize money. "I don't think my dad's too happy because we were going to go to Spain and I think we've got to go to Leicester now and play some Pro Tours," Littler added. "I've been checking the Pro Tour rankings and whoever is in 64th just keeps going up and up. If I don't qualify then I'm going to get grilled and if I do, I'll get grilled anyway." Former BDO world champion Mark Webster said he "half expects" the teenager to achieve the clean sweep, adding: "Who is going to stop Luke Littler?"

Beau Greaves won the Women's World Matchplay for the third time, coming through a thrilling last-leg decider to beat Fallon Sherrock 6-5 at Blackpool's Winter Gardens. The top seed was not at her best but, having been pushed all the way by Sherrock, held her nerve. Greaves let a 5-3 lead slip, and Sherrock hit a 180 in the deciding leg, but the 22-year-old responded with a maximum of her own, followed by a 145 set-up, before taking out 56 to seal the win. "I'm not one to celebrate but I just felt the relief after winning," Greaves told Sky Sports. "To hit that last dart was just an outpouring of relief. I am just so happy to win. I was nervous. That kind of pressure is a privilege."

Greaves came in as the clear favourite and breezed through her quarter-final, but found herself in trouble in the semis against Gemma Hayter, who took her to a deciding leg before Greaves produced a 104 checkout to reach the final. By contrast, Sherrock dropped only one leg en route to the trophy match and took out defending champion Lisa Ashton 5-1 in the semi-final. However, for the third year running she came up just short in the final; a first Women's Matchplay title since the inaugural tournament in 2022 continues to elude her. For three-time women's world champion Greaves, it is another major triumph in a year that already saw her become the first woman to win a PDC ranking title (beating Michael Smith in April) and the first woman to hit a nine-dart finish on the PDC ProTour (against Mensur Suljovic in February). "I knew before that playing women is just a little bit different for me now — I just try and concentrate on the men's game — but when I come back and play at this tournament it is hard and I knew it would be tough," Greaves added. "After last year's disappointment, I am so chuffed to get the win. The relief is so good for my game going forward."

stories.headline: Mayo ends 75-year All-Ireland drought with victory over Kerry
body: Mayo won the All-Ireland Senior Football Championship for the first time in 75 years on Sunday, defeating Kerry by three points at Croke Park in Dublin. The victory, witnessed by over 80,000 spectators, ended the so-called 'Mayo Curse' that had hung over the county since 1951 and gave Mayo its fourth All-Ireland title.

Kerry took an early lead when David Clifford scored a goal, but Mayo fought back to trail by just one point at half-time. Four minutes into the second half, Darragh Beirne finished a flowing move to put Mayo ahead, a lead they held to the final whistle. Mayo wore a white jersey for the first time in an All-Ireland final since 1951 due to a clash with Kerry's green home kit.

The origins of the 'curse' date to 1951, when Mayo last won the All-Ireland. According to legend, after the victory celebration, the team passed a funeral in Foxford and a local priest reportedly cursed them, saying they would never win again while any of those players were alive. The story was never confirmed, but Mayo lost 11 All-Ireland finals in the intervening decades. The last surviving member of the 1951 squad, Dr Mick Loftus, died in 2023 at age 93; Paddy Prendergast, the last player to feature in that final, died in 2021.

Emotion was high at the final whistle. Former Mayo defender Padraig O'Hora, working as a BBC pundit, said with tears in his eyes: 'Thousands upon thousands of people have dreamed of this day, I can't believe it's here.' Captain Jack Coyne, after delivering a speech, said: 'To every man, women, boy and girl in Mayo, wherever you are, dream big things. Anything is possible and we've shown it today.' Manager Andy Moran, in his first year in charge, went to his family in the stands.

Among the players was 18-year-old Kobe McDonald, who had 'one chance' written on his wrist. His father Ciaran played in previous All-Ireland final defeats. McDonald, who just finished his leaving cert exams, will move to Australia to join St Kilda in the Australian Football League. 'It's surreal, we don't know how to feel,' he said on the GAA Social. 'To look around and see the people, they have given us so much over the years and to give them something proper to shout about is special.'

Mayo will return to Castlebar in their home county for celebrations. The victory ends 75 years of hurt and heartbreak, and the county is expected to greet the team with a sea of celebration on Ireland's west coast.

stories.headline: Beltrán, Jones, Kent inducted into Baseball Hall of Fame
body: The National Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum welcomed three new members on Sunday, July 26, 2026, in Cooperstown, New York. The induction ceremony honored outfielders Carlos Beltrán and Andruw Jones, who were voted in by the Baseball Writers Association of America, and second baseman Jeff Kent, who was selected by the Hall of Fame's Contemporary Baseball Era Committee. The three-person class is the smallest since 2022, when Fred McGriff and Scott Rolen were inducted.

Beltrán, a nine-time All-Star and 1999 American League Rookie of the Year, entered the Hall in his fourth year on the ballot, receiving 84.2% of the vote. He retired with 2,725 hits, 435 home runs, and 312 stolen bases, joining Barry Bonds, Andre Dawson, Willie Mays, and Alex Rodriguez as the only players with 400 home runs and 300 stolen bases. Beltrán played for seven teams from 1998-2017, most notably with the Mets, whose cap he will wear on his plaque. He also won a World Series ring in 2017 with the Astros, though that legacy was tainted by the sign-stealing scandal. In his induction speech, Beltrán addressed Mets fans: 'Thank you for believing in me. You challenged me. You let me know when I needed to be better, and that was a lot of times. I got to hear those boos, but I also appreciate your support along the way.'

Andruw Jones, widely regarded as the best defensive center fielder of his generation, was inducted in his ninth year on the ballot, with his support rising from 7.3% in his first year to 78.4% this year. He won 10 straight Gold Gloves from 1998-2007 and slugged at least 26 home runs every year from 1998-2007, including a 51-homer season in 2005. Jones debuted with a historic playoff performance: at 19 years and 180 days, he became the youngest player ever to hit two home runs in a World Series game, doing so in Game 1 in 1996. He played for five teams from 1996-2012 and retired with 1,933 hits and 434 home runs. During his speech, Jones said, 'I never got to see Willie Mays play, so Ken Griffey was my guy. I wanted to be like him. For me and Carlos to join Griffey, Willie, and these other great center fielders in the Hall of Fame is hard to put into words for me.' He also acknowledged Braves legend Chipper Jones: 'Chipper pushed for my induction for many years. The Jones boys are in Cooperstown now.'

Jeff Kent, the 2000 National League MVP with the Giants, was voted in by the Contemporary Baseball Era Committee in December 2025, receiving 14 of 16 votes (12 required). He had exhausted his 10 years on the BBWAA ballot, never receiving more than 46.5% of the vote. Kent is one of the best-hitting second basemen in history, holding the record for most home runs by a primary second baseman with 377, and his 1,158 RBI rank third at the position. He played for six teams from 1992-2002, was a five-time All-Star, and won four Silver Sluggers. In his speech, Kent reflected on a bet with his father: 'If I were to earn a college scholarship, that he'd buy me a pickup truck... I quit racing and focused on school and baseball, and won that baseball scholarship. I got that truck. That truck is still with me.' He added, 'This day isn't about me. It's about baseball. It's a celebration of baseball and I just happen to be a part of it.'

The induction ceremony, held on the lawn outside the Clark Sports Center in Cooperstown, drew thousands of baseball fans. The Hall of Fame class of 2026 marks the culmination of years of voting for each inductee: Beltrán's support climbed from 46.5% in his first year to 84.2%, Jones rose from 7.3% to 78.4%, and Kent finally gained entry after falling short with the writers. All three are now enshrined in Cooperstown, joining the sport's all-time greats.

stories.headline: Norris wins Hungarian Grand Prix as Ferrari flounders
body: Lando Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix on Sunday, securing his first victory of the Formula 1 season in a drive he called 'one of my best performances.' The McLaren driver started from pole position but lost the lead to teammate Oscar Piastri on the first lap after sliding wide at Turn Two. Norris stayed calm, kept pace with Piastri in dirty air, and regained the lead after McLaren pitted Piastri to cover Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari, giving Norris clean air and a blistering pace. Piastri later retired with a gearbox failure, denying McLaren a one-two finish. Norris crossed the line ahead of Red Bull's Max Verstappen and championship leader Kimi Antonelli of Mercedes.

Norris described the performance as a product of hard work with his engineers to understand a car he called 'not an easy car to understand and figure out how to drive on the limit consistently.' He said, 'The pace advantage I had was huge today. But I don't know why. The cars are identical, and I've just been feeling very strong lately.' McLaren team principal Andrea Stella noted that Norris is 'much more confident' and 'more in control of his emotions,' adding, 'We've seen a great trajectory of development for Lando.' The win moves Norris to 98 points behind Antonelli in the drivers' standings, but Norris cautioned against expectations of a sustained title charge, saying, 'It doesn't mean if I'm quick here, we're going to be quick everywhere.'

Piastri, who appeared to direct anger at McLaren over team radio during the race, was actually furious with Williams driver Carlos Sainz after a collision while Piastri was lapping him. 'The timing of my stop was fine,' Piastri said. 'Without getting crashed into, I would have been ahead of Lando still.' He added, 'I don't really care if he didn't see me. The fact that he didn't and no-one told him, or there was a lack of complete awareness, is unacceptable.' Sainz said he had 'no idea I was trying to get lapped' and that it was 'impossible to avoid it.' Piastri's gearbox failure ended his race shortly after the incident.

Ferrari, pre-race favorites after topping Friday practice, endured a difficult Sunday. Charles Leclerc started alongside Norris on the front row but lost positions to Piastri, Verstappen, and Hamilton. Hamilton, who dropped from second to fifth on the grid with a penalty for impeding Piastri in qualifying, overtook Verstappen in the first pit stops only to be overtaken again when Verstappen made a 'brilliant move at Turn One that caught Hamilton napping.' A five-second penalty for pit-lane speeding left Hamilton behind Leclerc at the finish, the Ferraris fourth and fifth. Team boss Frederic Vasseur said, 'We made too many mistakes today, starting with the penalty and the fact that Max overtook us, that each time that we were doing a pit stop, we were losing a position for 0.2 or 0.3 seconds.' Hamilton, who remains second in the championship 50 points behind Antonelli, said, 'You can't make these kind of mistakes if you want to challenge for a title.'

Mercedes' George Russell had another difficult race, dropping to the back at the start due to an engine problem the team took blame for. He recovered to seventh but now trails Antonelli by 59 points. 'I'm sort of past the point of disappointment now,' Russell said. 'It's just unbelievable, the list of things that's happened this season.' Antonelli, who leads the championship, said, 'I did not expect to find myself in this position. But the car has been extremely good, the team has done an incredible job and, on my side, I try to maximise every opportunity I have.' The Hungarian Grand Prix marked the end of the first half of the season; the next race is the Dutch Grand Prix after F1's four-week summer break.

stories.headline: FDA Grants Full Approval to Selpercatinib for RET Fusion–Positive Solid Tumors
body: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has granted full approval to selpercatinib, marketed as Retevmo, for the treatment of patients aged 2 years and older with advanced solid tumors harboring a RET gene fusion. The approval, granted on July 14, marks a tumor-agnostic milestone in precision oncology, allowing the drug to be prescribed based on a shared genomic feature across diverse cancer types, including lung, thyroid, pancreatic, ovarian, and rare pediatric cancers.

Clinical trial findings demonstrated meaningful and sustained activity across more than a dozen cancer types. The objective response rate reached 47%, with nearly half of patients experiencing a substantial reduction in tumor size. Responses lasted for more than two years on average, an important finding among patients with advanced disease who had exhausted other available treatment options. Selpercatinib is a selective targeted therapy designed to inhibit abnormal RET signaling, blocking the pathway that supports cancer cell growth.

The FDA first granted accelerated approval to selpercatinib in 2020 for patients with advanced RET fusion–positive lung and thyroid cancers, based on clinical research led by Dr. Alexander Drilon and Dr. Eric Sherman at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center. Full approval was subsequently granted for those tumor-specific indications, and the accelerated approval was later expanded to include metastatic solid tumors with RET gene fusions regardless of site of origin, as well as patients as young as 2 years old. The latest regulatory action converts that tumor-agnostic indication from accelerated to full approval, confirming clinical benefit and safety for broader use.

The full approval highlights the growing importance of basket trials in oncology, which evaluate a treatment across multiple tumor types that share the same molecular alteration. According to Dr. Alexander Drilon, Chief of the Early Drug Development Service at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, the decision is a pivotal moment in precision oncology that reaffirms the value of conducting clinical trials based on tumor genetics rather than tumor location. Dr. Drilon led one of the two clinical trials supporting the FDA’s decision and noted that the approval expands treatment opportunities for patients with diverse tumor types, including rare cancers with few established options.

Research into selpercatinib is also moving into earlier stages of cancer. Dr. Drilon recently published findings showing that selpercatinib substantially reduced the risk of recurrence in patients with early-stage RET fusion–positive lung cancer, suggesting that targeted RET inhibition may eventually play a role in increasing the likelihood of cure for selected patients. The full approval reinforces the importance of comprehensive genomic testing in patients with advanced solid tumors, as RET fusions are rare—present in approximately 1% to 2% of lung cancers and 10% to 20% of papillary thyroid cancers—and may be missed unless tumors are tested using methods capable of detecting gene rearrangements.

stories.headline: Chinese AI models gain ground in US amid policy debate over competitiveness and security
body: Chinese artificial intelligence models are gaining popularity in the United States, driven by their affordability and efficiency, even as U.S. policymakers and tech companies debate potential restrictions. The latest catalyst was the July launch of Kimi K3 by Chinese startup Moonshot AI, which prompted San Francisco-based Mozilla CTO Raffi Krikorian to switch from Anthropic's Claude Fable, calling K3 "snappier." According to Sensor Tower, Kimi had more than 930,000 downloads globally in the week after K3's release, a 200% increase from the prior week, with U.S. downloads surging 387% to about 86,000. Moonshot temporarily suspended new subscriptions after demand pushed capacity near its limits.

The rise of Chinese models follows DeepSeek's debut in early 2024, which shook the U.S. tech industry with a model that performed on par with American counterparts at a fraction of the cost. Since then, startups Z.ai (Zhipu) and Moonshot have launched models in June and July, respectively, that experts say are nearly as intelligent as frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic. Alibaba previewed its Qwen3.8 Max in July, and DeepSeek rolled out previews of its V4 model in April. On OpenRouter, a platform tracking AI model usage, the top five most popular models over the past month were Chinese. U.S. companies such as cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase have said they are switching to Chinese models to cut costs.

The debate over Chinese AI has intensified in Washington, D.C., where OpenAI and Anthropic have reportedly lobbied regulators with concerns about open Chinese models. On the TechCrunch Equity podcast, journalist Kirsten Korosec noted that restrictions on Chinese open-weight models would primarily benefit a handful of U.S. frontier labs, asking: "Are we accelerating and ensuring that Americans win the AI race, or are we ensuring that certain frontier labs do better than others?" The discussion was sparked by a post from OpenAI's head of strategic futures, Dean Ball, who argued the U.S. should create regulatory "fear, uncertainty, and doubt" to hinder open-weight models' competitiveness—a position he later backed away from.

Most Chinese AI models are open-source, allowing anyone to examine and build on them, while leading U.S. models from Anthropic and OpenAI are closed-source. Mozilla's Krikorian observed that "the open frontier is becoming increasingly Chinese-built." U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned more sanctions could be coming to protect American intellectual property, and the Trump administration accused Moonshot of using "covert" methods to build K3 based on Anthropic's Fable—a claim Beijing rejects as "groundless." U.S. politicians and AI companies have accused Chinese startups of illicit "distillation" of their models, though no evidence of illegality has been presented.

Despite their gains, Chinese models still lag U.S. leaders in overall full-range capabilities, according to Anastasios Angelopoulos, CEO of AI evaluation platform Arena. However, Goldman Sachs wrote in a July report that Chinese models are reaching a "critical stage" for wide adoption, especially as demand for cost-effective AI agents grows. North Carolina technology executive Curt Meinhold, who prefers DeepSeek for tasks like finding business leads, said: "At the end of the day, most of us, 90 plus percent, don't need Mythos or Fable. We need something good enough." The U.S. is weighing whether to restrict Chinese AI models, a decision that could reshape the competitive landscape.

stories.headline: US charges American citizen for wiping phone at border
body: The US government is prosecuting American citizen Sam Tunick for allegedly wiping his phone when federal agents tried to seize it at Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson airport on January 24, 2025. Tunick is charged under a little-known and rarely used statute that makes it illegal to destroy or damage property to prevent authorities from seizing it. According to prosecutors, Tunick gave agents a “duress password” that triggered the phone’s factory reset instead of the actual passcode, using a feature of the privacy-focused operating system GrapheneOS.

Tunick’s attorneys argue that the detention and seizure were unlawful, and that agents questioned him about child exploitation images as “a pretext for a fishing expedition into Mr Tunick’s connections” to the Stop Cop City movement in Atlanta. The defense says agents refused to let Tunick speak to a lawyer, did not provide a warrant, and did not inform him of his legal rights. The government counters that a warrant was not required because Tunick had not yet been granted permission to enter the United States.

The case comes amid heightened scrutiny of travelers at US borders under the Trump administration, where even citizens can face hours-long detention and examination of social media accounts. Marlon Kautz, a member of the Atlanta Solidarity Fund, told the Guardian earlier this week that “we all have a right to secure our private data against unconstitutional searches. And we should — especially in a time of rising authoritarianism.” Most privacy advocates agree that the only way to protect data at the border is to delete it.

Tunick’s attorneys have filed a motion to toss all evidence, arguing that the detention and search were unlawful. The outcome of the case could set a precedent for the limits of border search authority and the rights of US citizens to protect their digital data from government seizure.

stories.headline: Apple plans smart glasses reveal at WWDC 2027, launch by year-end with privacy focus
body: Apple plans to unveil its first smart glasses at the Worldwide Developers Conference in June 2027, with a retail launch by the end of that year, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman. The company has pushed back an earlier target of early 2027 to refine both the product and its messaging around privacy.

The glasses are expected to rely on on-device processing and will omit features such as facial recognition or an always-on recording mode similar to Meta’s “super sensing.” Apple also will likely avoid using customer recordings to train its AI models, and it is not expected to adopt Meta’s practice of having contractors review user footage. Gurman reports that Apple may eventually release a version without a camera, or with a camera restricted to sensing only—similar to a rumored approach for Apple’s AI-enabled AirPods.

The privacy emphasis comes as Meta’s smart glasses have drawn criticism for enabling non-consensual video recording, with some calling them “pervert glasses.” Apple has spent more than a decade making privacy a defining product message, and entering the same category as Meta risks undermining that reputation regardless of how its approach differs. The company is reportedly working on additional hardware and software privacy features to address these concerns.

The delay to late 2027 gives Apple time to finalize its privacy features and the accompanying marketing narrative. The decision to steer clear of controversial capabilities—such as always-on recording or using customer data for AI training—is intended to differentiate Apple’s offering in a market that has become a flashpoint for consumer privacy debates.

stories.headline: SpaceX eyes tower catch for next Starship after 13th flight
body: SpaceX completed its 13th full-scale Starship test flight on Friday, sending the vehicle on a suborbital trajectory from South Texas to an intact splashdown in the Indian Ocean west of Australia. The 408-foot-tall (124-meter) Starship Version 3 rocket lifted off from Starbase, Texas, at 5:51 pm CDT (6:51 pm EDT; 22:51 UTC), powered by 33 methane-fueled Raptor engines on the Super Heavy booster. Unlike previous water landings that ended in fire, the ship gently tipped over and floated, allowing engineers to inspect its heat shield via drone for the first time. The more than 18,000 ceramic tiles withstood temperatures up to 2,600° Fahrenheit (1,430° Celsius) during reentry.

SpaceX communications manager Dan Huot called the intact splashdown a "dream scenario" for heat shield data collection. The company continued receiving signals from Starship after splashdown through its Starlink satellite network, and an onboard camera showed no external damage to the vehicle's six Raptor engines. SpaceX officials noted the flight subjected the vehicle to "significantly higher dynamic pressure" than previous missions. The intact vehicle opens the possibility of towing it to shore, likely in Australia, for further inspection, though Starship is not designed for saltwater exposure.

The Super Heavy booster, however, experienced a hard splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico after some engines failed to restart for the landing burn. SpaceX officials reported the booster completed the high-thrust portion of its boostback burn with all 33 engines for the first time with a Version 3 design, but a subset of engines ignited before the hard landing. The booster recovery remains a work in progress, as SpaceX previously recovered and re-flew Super Heavy boosters twice with the Version 2 design but not with Version 3.

During the flight, Starship deployed 20 upgraded Starlink V3 satellites from its payload bay using a Pez-like deployer. The satellites, which are larger and heavier than previous versions and cannot fit on Falcon 9 rockets, were designed to burn up on reentry. SpaceX ground teams established contact with each satellite via radio and laser links and downloaded key telemetry before their destruction. The ship also performed a brief 14-second restart of one Raptor engine, visible from South Africa, which SpaceX hailed as a "core capability for future orbital missions."

Elon Musk wrote on X Friday evening that, barring problems discovered in mission data review, SpaceX will attempt to catch the ship with the launch tower on the next flight. This would involve sending Starship on a longer-range trajectory, possibly into low-Earth orbit, and returning it to the launch site for capture by mechanical arms—a feat already accomplished with the Super Heavy booster. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman praised the mission, writing that Starship's capabilities will be "game-changing" for lunar exploration. NASA is working with SpaceX and Blue Origin to develop human-rated landers for the Artemis program, which requires orbital refueling—a capability that will demand multiple Starship launches and rapid reuse from multiple pads.

Shana Diez, SpaceX's director of Starship flight reliability, described the flight as collecting "really critical data" on the deorbit burn and first flight of next-generation Starlink satellites. "It feels like we are ready to kick into gear on delivering payload to orbit," she wrote on X. SpaceX has one active launch pad in Texas, a second under renovation there, and two more under construction in Florida. The company's iterative development program now appears poised to move toward orbital missions and operational Starlink V3 deployments, which promise higher-speed direct-to-device connectivity for consumers and the US military.
